title: Ghosts of Lessons Past Pt 4
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien continues his series of reflections on his early teaching, auditing three lessons built around student engagement, group choice and novelty. He recalls a taste-perception station rotation in psychology, a plan-the-perfect-murder starter in legal studies, and a choose-your-own-nation trade presentation in economics, all inspired by his initial teacher education. For each he shows how much time and money went into activities that created the appearance of learning, then states what he would do now. His answer is consistently to teach the content explicitly, keeping a small hook such as the green-ketchup story and replacing the open-ended task with scenario questions or direct instruction. The piece ends by naming the cost: learning time lost to generic skills and learning-styles thinking, with Coe's engagement-as-poor-proxy argument as the unspoken backdrop.
points: Engagement-driven lessons can give an outside observer the illusion of learning while students do very little thinking about the content.
Open group tasks with free choice of format produce wildly varying outputs that make marking close to meaningless.
The retained kernel of a novelty lesson is usually a short story plus explicit teaching, with a written task to check understanding.
Initial teacher education pushed learning styles, differentiation and student-chosen group work, and the author now counts the lost learning time as the real cost.
The what-would-I-do-now format turns past mistakes into a practical template for converting activity-based lessons into explicit ones.
quotes: When I first began teaching I clearly did not value my time or income very much. What I did value was doing whatever I could to increase the “engagement” of my classes.

Strangely, teenagers were incredibly engaged in this activity despite its dubious nature. The way in which they diligently worked on their plan for the whole time would give an outside observer the illusion that learning was happening in the room.

The level of variance in these presentations was high to say the least. We had a pre-recorded news program in front of a green screen, standard oral presentations and even a role play of a business meeting for some reason. They were certainly memorable (well at least the good ones were) but the time and effort which went into creating some incredibly shallow learning was questionable at best.

One thing that I do commend my past self on is that I at least had the students complete both a self-reflection of their contribution to the group as well as a judgement of other group members contributions to the group which I used alongside my own observations when creating individual marks. However, with the variety of ways the students presented their information the marks I was giving were likely pretty meaningless and more based on how much I enjoyed their presentation.

Literally just teach them. Explicit teaching about Australia’s trade relationship with China while also peppering in some of the concepts which become relevant in their senior years such as the impact of trade on exchange rates, the balance of payments etc to ensure they understand the importance of trade and the impact it has on our economy in totality.

I often wonder what more I could have done for these students if I was able to teach them with what I know now. It is scary to think about all of the learning time that was wasted under the guise of building generic skills or appealing to different learning styles. Obviously, I was just trying to do the best I could with the information I knew at the time but I’m glad I know better now.
